y-m-48-04.title: Test saying ‘if square bigger, number bigger’
y-m-48-04.topic: Counterexamples and extra condition making proposition true
y-m-48-04.goal: Make counterexample; find conditions that ensure claim; explain using signs and squares.
y-m-48-04.material: For real a,b, Hyunwoo says ‘If a²>b², then a>b.’ He tested (3,2) and (5,1). (a² read a squared.) 3 2 5 1

y-m-48-04.s.s2.explain: If a≥0, a²>b² gives a=|a|>|b|≥b, so true. Both positive is stronger, also true. Other conditions leave (−3,1) counterexample. 0 3 1

y-m-48-04.s.s2.acc.1: Both positive sufficient; you missed weaker a≥0 alone also works.

y-m-48-04.s.s3.model.1: a²>b² means |a|>|b|, comparing magnitudes only. If a can be negative, a>b may fail, so add condition a≥0.

y-m-48-06.title: Wetin be opposite of 'everybody like am'?
y-m-48-06.goal: Make negation of statements wey contain 'all' and 'or', then test wrong negation inside class where p dey true to show the mistake.
y-m-48-06.material: We survey 10 students for one class (universal set U). M na students wey like math, E na students wey like English. Statement p: 'Every student like math or English' (here 'or' include person wey like both). Negation of statement na another statement wey dey false when original true, and true when original false. Sua make negation of p like below. (Mᶜ we read 'complement of M', ∩ mean intersection, ∪ mean union, ∅ na empty set.)
y-m-48-06.thinking.1: Test using meaning of negation (truth value always opposite)
y-m-48-06.thinking.2: Build arrangement wey act as counterexample
y-m-48-06.prereq.1: Meaning of statements wey contain 'all' and 'some'
y-m-48-06.prereq.2: Meaning of union M∪E, complement, and intersection
y-m-48-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line for Sua working.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine class with students wey like only math, only English, and both; check each line if e true or false inside that class.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.hint.1: For class where p true, negation of p must be false. For every line, test whether e true or false for that kind class.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.0: p: Every student dey inside M∪E. That mean M∪E=U.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.1: For the negation, change 'all' to 'some' and negate the condition after am too.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.2: Negation of 'like math or English' na 'no like math and no like English'.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.3: So negation of p: Some student no like math or no like English.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.4: For set language, we fit write Mᶜ∪Eᶜ≠∅ (no be empty set).
y-m-48-06.s.s1.explain: Line 3 wrong. Negation of 'like math or English' na 'like neither math nor English' (negating 'or' give 'and'). So line 4 and 5 wrong too. Correct negation na 'Some student like neither math nor English', and for sets, Mᶜ∩Eᶜ≠∅. Lines 1 and 2 correct.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.prompt: We wan show say Sua negation (line 4) no be exact opposite of p. Make 3 different classes where p true but Sua negation too true. All 10 students, and each like at least one of math or English. m na number wey like only math, e na only English, b na both.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.hint.0: First decide how many students wey like neither go make p true.

y-m-48-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Number of students must be integer wey be 0 or more.

y-m-48-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The total no be 10. For p to be true, all 10 students must like at least one of the two.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.ok.c3: One student no like one of math or English, so Sua negation na true.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.fail.c3: All 10 students like both, so Sua negation na false.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.explain: For example, if (m, e, b)=(5, 5, 0), all 10 students like one of the two, so p true. Some students too no like one of math or English, so Sua negation also true. Negation wey no false when p true no be exact negation.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.prompt: Which one be the correct negation of p?
y-m-48-06.s.s3.hint.0: Use class arrangements from the step before; check whether each option true when p true, and remove options wey true.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.hint.1: Make one class by yourself where p false, then check which choices true for that class.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.o.a: Every student like neither math nor English
y-m-48-06.s.s3.r.a: You leave 'all' as e be. Even if only some students like neither, p false.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.o.b: Some student no like math or no like English
y-m-48-06.s.s3.r.b: Na the negation Sua make. For the earlier (5, 5, 0), e true at the same time as p.

y-m-48-06.s.s3.o.d: Every student no like math or no like English

y-m-48-07.title: If you check plenty examples, e become proof?
y-m-48-07.topic: Statements with 'all', counterexamples, and the limits of checking examples
y-m-48-07.goal: Use step-by-step data understand say checking some values no fit prove 'for every n' statement, but one counterexample fit make am false; explain difference from statement about existence.
y-m-48-07.material: Call this statement q. q: 'For every natural number n, n²+n+41 na prime number.' (We read n² as 'n squared'. Prime number na natural number bigger than 1 wey only 1 and itself fit divide am.) The data go show one part at a time.
y-m-48-07.thinking.0: Tell checking examples apart from proving
y-m-48-07.thinking.1: Adjust how sure you dey according to new data
y-m-48-07.thinking.2: Compare how examples work for 'for all' and 'there exists' statements
y-m-48-07.prereq.1: Meaning of prime number and how to test prime numbers
y-m-48-07.s.s1.prompt: Data dey show bit by bit. Every time, choose wetin you think about q.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.hint.0: Tell whether data for each step cover all natural number n or only some of dem.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.hint.1: Do new data calculation yourself, check say e match the values dem give.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.info: When we put n=1, 2, 3, 4, 5, n²+n+41 give 43, 47, 53, 61, 71; all of dem na prime.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin you think about q now?
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.after: The five results give clue say q fit be true, but dem no cover 'every natural number n', so dem no be proof.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: All five na prime, so q don prove
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Five na only some of all natural numbers. We still no know whether e work for n wey we never put inside.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Prime numbers dey show one after another by chance, so q probably false
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Prime numbers one after another na clue wey support q. Clue no be reason to declare am false too.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: q fit be true, but dem never prove am
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The five values give no information at all
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: E dey support q being true. But the main thing be say e no be proof.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.info: Computer calculate everything from n=1 to 39, and all dem be prime.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: Wetin you go do now? Choose the suitable actions. (You fit choose more than one.)
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.after: Testing next value directly (to search for counterexample) and finding reason e work for every n (proving) both suitable. Checking 39 values fit make you believe am more, but e no prove q.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: All 39 correct, so treat q as proved and stop
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even 39 na only some of all natural numbers. Number of values checked no be standard for proof.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Calculate next values directly, like n=40 and 41
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Look inside the expression for reason e be prime, then try explain am
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Think say 40th one likely correct too, so no need check again
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Something wey likely different from something wey true. Counterexample fit show for value wey you never check.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now wetin we fit talk about q?
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.after: When n=40, n²+n+41=41×41 no be prime, so q false. One counterexample dey make 'for all n' statement false. n=41 composite too, so removing only one exception no go fix am.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Na prime for most n, so treat q as almost true and use am like that
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: 'For all n' statement false if even one case fail. 'Most' no be wetin q talk.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Fix am by remove only n=40 as exception: 'if n no be 40, e be prime'; then e true
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: n=41 too give 41²+41+41=41×43, wey composite. If you fix statement by removing one exception, you must test am again.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 1681 fit be calculation mistake, so delay the judgment
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You fit check 41×41 by multiplying directly. If you fit check one calculation, check am before judging.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.reflect: How your confidence in q change for steps 1, 2, and 3? Which information only make you more sure, and which information end the judgment? Write how this difference connect to the difference between 'plenty examples dey' and 'one example dey'.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.prompt: Make q' mean 'there is one natural number n wey n²+n+41 na composite number (number bigger than 1 wey no be prime)'. From only step 3 information, wetin we fit talk about q'?
y-m-48-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write with words wetin kind n q' need to be true, then check whether 40 meet the condition.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.hint.1: Put side by side the role n=40 get for q and q', then compare.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.a: Only n=40 dey enough to settle say q' true
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.b: Need check more n to know if true or false.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.r.b: q' is an existence claim, so one example enough to make am true. Check if 40 such example.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.c: False, because most n give primes.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.r.c: Existence claim asks if even one example dey, no be whether most are.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.d: We no fit call am true. Counterexample relates to q, not q'.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.r.d: Same n=40 counterexample becomes example for q'. Notice both statements use same value differently.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.explain: q (‘for all n’) false with one counterexample; q' (‘some n exists’) true with one supporting example. But any number of examples no prove q true.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.prompt: Friend checks n=1 to 10 all prime and says ‘Proof done!’ Tell them why not enough and next step, without discouraging.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.hint.0: Put checked n range beside all n in q, compare.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.hint.1: Choose next n to test and give reason one line.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You credit friend's effort and clarify checking isn't proof?
y-m-48-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You suggest exactly what value to test or how to prove?
y-m-48-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You state judgment accurately without claiming q false?
y-m-48-07.s.s3.model.0: Checking 10 values is good start, but larger n may not be prime. Try n=40 for counterexample, or reason why every n works.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.model.1: Ten primes suggest q may be right. We haven't checked all naturals, so test larger n or prove reason.

y-m-48-08.title: Two friends' set equalities: who right?
y-m-48-08.topic: Set operation laws: difference set relation to union/intersection
y-m-48-08.goal: Use one example to disprove false equality; find element types causing failure, and plan check to trust equality always.
y-m-48-08.material: A,B,C sets. A−B means elements in A not B. Jimin says A−(B∪C)=(A−B)∪(A−C) always; Doyun says A−(B∪C)=(A−B)∩(A−C) always. ∪ union; ∩ intersection.
y-m-48-08.thinking.1: Split cases by element membership type
y-m-48-08.prereq.2: Think whether element belongs to set.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.prompt: You tested both equalities with A={1,2,3,4}, B={1,2}, C={2,3}. Best lesson? 1 2 3 4 1 2 2 3
y-m-48-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write sides of both expressions using these sets and compare.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.a: Both hold in this example, so always hold.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.r.a: Calculate Jimin sides yourself. One example working no prove always.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.b: Doyun works here, so always; Jimin false.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.r.b: Right that Jimin false, but one example can't show Doyun always.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.c: One example can't decide either equality.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.r.c: One example can disprove ‘always’. Calculate Jimin equality here.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.d: Jimin false; Doyun only worked in this example.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.prompt: Find element types making Jimin fail. Let x get 1 if in A,B,C respectively, else 0; write (a,b,c). Enter different triples where x belongs to exactly one of A−(B∪C) and (A−B)∪(A−C).
y-m-48-08.s.s2.hint.0: Say what x∉B∪C means for B,C, then where x lies in A−B and A−C.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.hint.1: Table 8 possible triples (a,b,c); find rows where sides differ.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.ok.c2: x belongs to exactly one set.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.fail.c2: x belongs both or neither; equality works for that type.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.explain: If (a,b,c)=(1,1,0), x in B∪C, so not in A−(B∪C); but x not in C, so in A−C and therefore union side. (1,0,1) same. Any set example with one such element breaks Jimin equality. 1 1 0 1 0 1
y-m-48-08.s.s3.prompt: What should you check to trust Doyun equality always?
y-m-48-08.s.s3.hint.0: Count total cases from x membership in A,B,C.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.hint.1: Define both sides in words using ‘belongs to’ and see if statements match.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.o.a: Try 2–3 more set examples and compare sides.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.r.a: Even more examples don't test all cases. They build confidence, no guarantee.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.o.b: Shade one Venn region and check equality.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.r.b: One region represents only part of 8 cases.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.o.c: Check both sides' membership same for all 8 (a,b,c) cases.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.o.d: Rewrite left as ‘in A, and in neither B nor C’; compare in words to right side.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.r.d: Unpacking definitions in words is valid proof; it does same as checking all 8 cases differently.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.explain: Only 8 element membership types exist. If sides match all, equality always holds. Explaining same meaning from definitions is equally valid.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.acc.0: Word-based definition proof is valid, same work as checking all 8 cases.

y-m-48-09.title: If n² even, is n even?
y-m-48-09.goal: Choose which of 3 solutions is valid; explain to middle-school student why contrapositive proves original; tell apart claims where method works.
y-m-48-09.material: Three students prove r: natural n, if n² even then n even. (n² read n squared; even=2k, odd=2k+1.)
y-m-48-09.prereq.2: Relation between contrapositive and truth value
y-m-48-09.s.s1.prompt: Three students claim proof of r. Choose all valid proofs.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.hint.0: Compare n values each solution handles.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.hint.1: Write what Hajun/Jiyu assume and conclude; compare with r.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.o.a: Seoa: Checked n=1 to 10 where n² even; got 2,4,6,8,10, all even; therefore r true. 1 10 2 4 6 8 10
y-m-48-09.s.s1.r.a: n≥11 untested. Some checking no proof.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.o.b: Jiyu: n²=n×n. Odd×odd is odd, so if n odd, n² odd. Therefore r true.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.r.b: Logic direction right, but assumes odd×odd=odd known. Was it proved?
y-m-48-09.s.s1.o.c: Hajun: if n odd, n=2k+1, k integer; n²=2(2k²+2k)+1 odd, therefore r true.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.explain: Seoa checked some cases only. Hajun directly proved contrapositive ‘odd n gives odd n²’ with 2k+1. Jiyu uses same contrapositive assuming odd×odd=odd; prove it by expanding (2k+1)(2m+1) to complete proof.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.acc.0: Jiyu (b) uses same logic as Hajun if odd×odd=odd accepted. Showing that fact separately makes it complete.
y-m-48-09.s.s2.prompt: Your middle-school grade 3 younger sibling asks why prove odd n case instead of r directly. Use Hajun solution explain simply; include why write 2k+1.
y-m-48-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write hypothesis/conclusion of r, compare to Hajun proposition's hypothesis/conclusion.
y-m-48-09.s.s2.hint.1: Why hard to decide n² parity without writing odd number with a letter?
y-m-48-09.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. Instead of starting with n² even, ...
y-m-48-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: You say ‘odd n implies odd n²’ is equivalent to r?
y-m-48-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Explain 2k+1 (so can calculate) at sibling level?
y-m-48-09.s.s2.model.0: r and ‘odd n implies odd n²’ have same truth (contrapositive), so prove that. Any odd is 2k+1 for integer k; square and see it is 2×integer+1, hence odd.
y-m-48-09.s.s2.model.1: Starting n²=2m makes n form hard to know. Equivalent contrapositive starts odd n=2k+1; square has remainder 1, hence odd.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.hint.0: List small n=1..12 satisfying hypothesis; check conclusion too.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.hint.1: If no counterexample, try negating conclusion and showing hypothesis fails.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.o.a: If n² multiple of 4, n multiple of 4.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.r.a: n=2 gives n²=4 multiple 4, but 2 not multiple 4.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.o.c: If n² multiple of 9, n multiple of 9.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.r.c: n=3 gives 9 multiple of 9, but 3 not multiple 9.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.o.d: If n² multiple of 3, n multiple of 3.
y-m-48-09.s.s3.explain: Odd n means n³ odd, so b true. If n not divisible by 3, n=3k±1 and n²=3(...)+1, not multiple 3, so d true. a counterexample n=2; c counterexample n=3.
